transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-04
Start: 10:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Omar (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM), Maya (Summit Head of ML), Liam (Platform), Rita (Data Eng)

Summary:
Weekly POC sync focusing on caching (prefix + KV cache) hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, configuration tweaks, and next steps for a 24h benchmark on dedicated nodes. Customer saw improvement after key-normalization but still below target; discussed TTLs, LRU thrashing, and prompt templating to increase reuse.

Topics:
- Current hit rates and telemetry (hot keys, percentiles)
- Key normalization / canonicalization approach
- TTL and eviction policy tradeoffs
- Prompt reuse strategies and templating
- Bench plan and rollout steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh, quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya: Hi Maya here.
[00:07] Liam: Liam, yep.
[00:09] Rita: Rita.
[00:11] Omar: Omar from Redwood SE.
[00:12] Ava: Great, thanks. So quick agenda - run through the numbers Omar sent, talk tuning, then actions.

[02:00] Omar: Alright, I pulled the telemetry from last 72 hours. After we applied the initial key normalization rules last week, the KV cache hit rate moved from ~28% to about 56% at the 95th percentile of requests. Prefix cache hit is around 48% average, though there's a big tail. So pretty good, but still room to improve toward the 70% target we discussed.
[02:30] Maya: Uh that matches what we saw, we, we do see a lot of session-specific noise - user ids and ephemeral tokens were making keys unique. The normalization helped but there's still some chatter from long prompt prefixes.
[03:10] Rita: Quick Q, are those numbers global or per-shard? Because our traffic is sharded and some shards are much hotter.
[03:16] Omar: Good question - those aggregates are global but I included per-shard breakdown in the spreadsheet. The hot shard has a KV hit of about 62% and a cold shard ~34%. LRU eviction on the cold shards is thrashing during peak.
[04:00] Liam: We suspect it's because session ids are embedded in the first 40 tokens of the prefix, so the prefix cache is almost never reused.
[04:20] Ava: So two parallel knobs - normalize keys to strip or hash session ids, and reduce prefix variability by templating prompts. Omar, what did you change for normalization specifically?
[04:30] Omar: We added regex rules to drop user-specific UUIDs and timestamp-like tokens, and we truncated dynamic metadata beyond the first n tokens. Also changed hashing to use a stable Murmur hash instead of naive concatenation - that cut collisions and mismatched keys.
[05:05] Maya: There's a small transcription note - I think someone put "Murmur" as "murmur" in the doc, so ignore the casing - but yeah, the hash change really lowered key explosion.
[05:30] Rita: After that, TTL settings - we currently have a 10-minute default TTL for KV entries. Do we expect to increase? We saw cost increase if TTL is too high.
[05:45] Omar: Right. In our micro-bench, moving to 30-40 minute TTL increased hit rate by ~10 points but increased memory utilization ~1.6x on the cache nodes in the Dedicated config. There's a tradeoff. We suggested a 20-minute default with hot-key pinning for top 5% as compromise.
[06:30] Liam: Pinning top keys makes sense for the hot shard. Also maybe tiered TTLs by route.
[06:40] Ava: Good. What about eviction - you mentioned LRU thrashing, any configuration changes?
[06:47] Omar: We bumped eviction window to a segmented LRU with per-shard quotas; that reduced cross-shard evictions. Also enabling admission filters so very large embedded blobs don't evict many small useful keys.
[07:15] Maya: Ok, I like admission filters. One question about instrumentation - can we get latency-by-hit vs miss, and cost per 1k requests? The deck had rough numbers but we need per-route.
[07:30] Omar: Yep, I can export latency histograms split by hit/miss and per-route cost estimate. I'll include that in the dashboard link.
[08:00] Rita: Any impact on model output quality from caching? We worry reusing prefix responses might surface stale context.
[08:10] Omar: We only cache deterministic parts - prefix embeddings and KV of repeated system messages and commonly reused prompt fragments. For completions we cache only when request match equals above a threshold and model temperature is low/zero. So quality impact should be minimal. We ran a spot check of 500 queries - 0.6% divergence in top-1 when caching was enabled, mostly acceptable.
[08:50] Maya: That's fine, our app can tolerate small divergence if latency and cost improve.
[09:10] Ava: Let's talk prompt reuse strategy - what concrete steps?
[09:20] Omar: Three recommendations: 1) canonicalize prompt templates (strip user ids, sort meta fields), 2) separate system + user messages and cache system outputs where stable, 3) standardize chunking for long context so prefix starts align across requests.
[10:00] Liam: For canonicalization, do you expect we change template rendering on our side or can Redwood do on the proxy?
[10:10] Omar: Either is possible. Best for performance if you do canonicalization at the application layer before sending, but Redwood can apply lightweight normalization at the edge as a fallback. We'll share the regex rules and a small lib you can run.
[10:40] Rita: Any concerns with PII? We're still under SOC 2 review and some of these prefixes include personal data.
[10:48] Priya: We recommend redaction first - strip PII before caching and we can integrate with your KMS policies. We'll add redaction steps to the runbook.
[11:05] Maya: Ok great. What about the bench run plan?
[11:10] Omar: Plan: run 24h on dedicated nodes using your peak traffic trace. Two config variants: A) TTL=20m + top-keys pinned + canonicalization; B) TTL=40m + aggressive pinning. We'll collect hit-rate, per-token latency, memory usage, and cost estimate.
[11:35] Maya: Do we need additional capacity for the bench?
[11:38] Ava: For the 40m variant maybe burst capacity. I can share pricing for a 48-hour dedicated burst slot.
[11:45] Omar: Also we'll enable detailed tracing for the bench to capture per-request cache decisions. That will add small overhead but needed for analysis.
[12:05] Liam: Sounds good. Anything else on eviction algorithm choice? We talked about segmented LRU vs CLOCK.
[12:12] Omar: SegLRU with per-shard quotas looked best in our tests. CLOCK had slightly better throughput but worse hit rates on skewed workloads.
[12:30] Rita: One practical note - our codebase generates slightly different whitespace in templates and that breaks simple string keys. Maybe normalization should collapse whitespace.
[12:36] Omar: Yep we'll add whitespace collapse and lowercasing to the rules. Also canonicalize punctuation.
[13:05] Maya: Ok recap of decisions?
[13:10] Ava: Recap - continue normalization + hashing, set default TTL to 20m with top-5% pinning, apply admission filters and segmented LRU per-shard, implement prompt templating and whitespace/punct normalization, run 24h bench A/B on dedicated nodes, export latency-by-hit dashboards, and share pricing for burst capacity.
[13:40] Rita: Looks good. Couple of risks: memory cost in Dedicated and slight output divergence; we accept with limits.
[13:55] Ava: Great. Next steps - action items we'll capture.

End of transcript.
